summary: Ray Myers, chief architect at All Hands AI (makers of OpenHands), frames his talk around empathy and listening rather than pure technology, describing his recurring role as an AI skeptic. He questions Dario Amodei's claim that AI will write essentially all code in 12 months, noting LLMs break old code and perform far better writing new code than maintaining existing code — a doubly ignored limitation. He recounts emotionally charged reactions to his skepticism, including being called a liar and hearing 'resistance is futile' — a Borg villain quote. He identifies six endgame scenarios: extreme completion (already happening via Cursor, Copilot, and short-leash agents), dev apocalypse (developers unnecessary; desirable if feasible but feasibility is the real objection), abstraction leap (current code becomes like assembly), uncharted waters (foundation not code-like, e.g., model inference as computation or superintelligent AI inventing new paradigms), review economy (cheap AI PRs but humans stuck reviewing them — a pit stop, not an endgame, signaling unmanaged bottlenecks addressable via theory of constraints), and infinite pile of garbage (coding assistants explode tech debt faster than value). For abstraction leap, Myers covers 'prompts as code' (predictability concerns, Parcel paper generating a 220-line Lisp interpreter) and DSLs (CSS, SQL, regex, Excel as examples; language workbenches like JetBrains MPS, XText, Racket; LLMs may improve cost-benefit tradeoff). Evidence on quality is contradictory: Uplevel found higher bug rates without better throughput; Getclear found copy-paste exceeding refactoring for the first time in 2024; GitHub found Copilot improves quality on fixed tasks. Myers notes all sources have something to sell and calls for rigorous independent academic studies. Scenarios interrelate — extreme completion could slide into infinite pile of garbage; combining DSLs with extreme completion could work well. Different industries will be impacted differently. Myers closes by stressing we are active builders, not passive observers, and must decide what we want from software: no programmers vs. everyone a programmer, quality vs. quantity, and how to treat people whose skills become obsolete.

sections.title: Introduction and Framing as Empathy Talk
sections.summary: Myers introduces himself as chief architect at All Hands AI, makers of OpenHands. He frames the talk as being about empathy and listening rather than AI or programming specifically.

sections.title: The AI Skeptic's Experience
sections.summary: Myers describes his role as AI skeptic, citing Amodei's claim that AI will write essentially all code in 12 months. He raised a mainframe replacement challenge and repeatedly notes LLMs break old code and perform better on new code than existing code. He recounts being called a liar, told he has his head in the sand, and warned he will be left behind. He critiques 'resistance is futile' as a Borg villain quote and references Picard/Locutus from Star Trek.

sections.title: Six Endgame Scenarios Introduction
sections.summary: Myers introduces six scenarios embedded in current discourse: extreme completion, dev apocalypse, abstraction leap, uncharted waters, review economy, and infinite pile of garbage.

sections.title: Extreme Completion
sections.summary: The most conservative scenario, already happening. Autocomplete-style editors like Cursor and Copilot continue helping with typing. Even multi-step agents remain on an engineer's leash. Demonstrations include Cursor generating a Haskell function and OpenHands producing a 48-file PR via Slack. Myers notes Haskell's strong type system as a counterbalance to LLM uncertainty.

sections.title: Dev Apocalypse
sections.summary: Developers become unnecessary; non-developers see this as innovator's paradise. Myers argues if feasible it would be desirable — programming fulfilling its destiny, finishing the project of computer science. The real objection is feasibility, not desirability. Critics can dismiss skeptics as just wanting to keep their jobs.

sections.title: Abstraction Leap: Prompts as Code and DSLs
sections.summary: Current code becomes like assembly language; most work happens at a higher abstraction. 'Prompts as code' makes natural language the main artifact but faces predictability objections. The Parcel paper generates a 220-line Python Lisp interpreter from 61 lines of structured prompts, but Myers doubts this is a solved problem for real applications. DSLs (CSS, SQL, regex, Excel) are a more promising flavor; language workbenches (JetBrains MPS, Lion Web, XText, Racket) have improved risk-reward over 20 years, and LLMs may further improve it. Myers declares 'the year of DSLs' on his YouTube channel Craft versus Craft. Underneath the abstraction, code remains fundamentally code-like.

sections.title: Uncharted Waters
sections.summary: Some argue the future foundation will not be code-like — direct model inference as new computation, or superintelligent AI inventing paradigms we cannot conceive. Myers considers these possible but says we must chart and prove them before planning seriously; nothing like this has proven out yet.

sections.title: Review Economy
sections.summary: Cheap AI-generated PRs flood developers who are stuck manually reviewing them — the least fun part of the job becoming the whole job. Myers sees this as a pit stop, not an endgame, signaling unmanaged bottlenecks. He recommends theory of constraints (Eli Goldratt, 'The Goal') and shifting left via type theory or prioritization — shipping a third of items for 90% of value.

sections.title: Infinite Pile of Garbage
sections.summary: The most dismal scenario: coding assistants explode tech debt faster than value, digging a hole even AI cannot escape. Uplevel's controlled trial found higher bug rates without better throughput. Getclear's white paper found 2024 was the first year copy-pasted code exceeded refactored code — a code quality red flag. GitHub found the opposite (Copilot improves quality) but on a fixed-task controlled experiment. Myers notes all sources have something to sell and calls for rigorous independent academic studies.

sections.title: Scenarios Interrelate and Closing
sections.summary: Scenarios interrelate: extreme completion could slide past dev apocalypse into infinite pile of garbage; combining DSLs with extreme completion could work well. Different industries will be impacted differently. Myers closes by stressing we are active builders, not passive observers — we must decide what we want from software: no programmers vs. everyone a programmer, quality vs. quantity, and how to treat people whose skills become obsolete.
